title: Does Forgiving Other People Actually Help You?
metaTitle: Does Forgiving Other People Actually Help You?
metaDescription: Research broadly links forgiveness to lower stress and better wellbeing — for the forgiver. But forgiveness means letting go of resentment, not excusing harm.
keyFinding: Research broadly suggests forgiveness tends to benefit the forgiver — linked to lower anxiety, depression, and stress — but in this work forgiveness means letting go of resentment for your own sake, not excusing harm, forgetting, reconciling, or staying in an unsafe situation.
honestAnswer: On balance, yes — but with one crucial qualification about what 'forgiveness' actually means. The research broadly suggests that forgiveness tends to benefit the person doing the forgiving, with links to lower anxiety, depression, and stress and to better physical-health markers. A likely mechanism is that it reduces rumination and chronic resentment, which are themselves hard on the mind and body.

The qualification matters as much as the finding. In this research, forgiveness means releasing resentment and the wish for revenge for your own sake. It does not mean excusing what happened, forgetting it, reconciling with the person, or staying in a situation that is harmful or unsafe. Forgiveness in the studied sense is something internal you can do even with someone you never see again — and forced or premature forgiveness can backfire rather than help.
whatDataShows: A substantial body of research, including work by Everett Worthington and by Loren Toussaint and colleagues, links forgiveness to better mental health — lower anxiety, depression, and stress — and to some better physical-health markers. The effects are generally modest and correlational in much of the work, but the direction is fairly consistent across studies, and some intervention research suggests structured forgiveness work can actually shift these outcomes rather than merely correlate with them.

A commonly proposed mechanism is the reduction of rumination and chronic resentment. Holding onto an unresolved grievance tends to keep replaying it, which sustains stress responses over time; releasing the resentment appears to interrupt that loop. In this framing the benefit comes less from anything that happens to the other person and more from what stops happening inside the forgiver.

The definition is doing heavy lifting here, and the research is careful about it. Forgiveness in this work means letting go of resentment and the desire to retaliate — explicitly not excusing the harm, denying it mattered, forgetting it, reconciling, or remaining in an unsafe situation. Some studies also find that forgiveness pushed too early or under pressure can backfire, which is why researchers treat it as a process rather than a single decision or a thing one is obligated to perform.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Forgiveness is widely framed as something you do for the other person — a gift, a letting-them-off-the-hook — which makes it feel unfair when you have been genuinely wronged. The research reframes it as primarily self-directed: the main beneficiary in the data is the forgiver, which is a very different proposition from absolving someone who does not deserve it.

It also gets conflated with reconciliation, excusing, or forgetting, and those conflations are exactly what make it feel impossible or even dangerous in serious cases. Releasing your own resentment is a separate act from re-entering a relationship or pretending the harm did not happen — you can do the first without ever doing the others.

And resentment can feel protective, as if holding onto it guards against being hurt again or honours the seriousness of what happened. Part of why letting go feels wrong is that it can seem like dropping your guard or minimising the wrong — even though, in the research, releasing resentment and staying clear-eyed about what happened are not in conflict.
whatResearchSaysToDo: Where structured approaches have been studied, forgiveness tends to be treated as a gradual process rather than a one-off decision. Worthington's widely used REACH model is one such framework, walking through recalling the hurt honestly, building empathy or understanding where possible, and committing to release resentment over time — with the emphasis on it being for the forgiver's own benefit, not the offender's.

The research broadly favours acknowledging the harm fully before any letting-go — naming that it was real and that it mattered — rather than skipping to forgiveness. Approaches that honour the seriousness of the wrong, and that separate releasing resentment from reconciling, are the ones more consistent with healthy outcomes in the literature.

Working on reducing rumination is a closely related, well-supported lever, since chronic replaying of a grievance is part of what keeps it costly. To the extent that forgiveness helps, much of its value seems to come through quieting that loop — so anything that genuinely reduces the rumination tends to point in the same beneficial direction.
whatDoesNotHelp: Forced or premature forgiveness does not help and may make things worse. Some research finds that forgiving under pressure, or before genuinely processing the harm, can backfire — for example by leaving anger unaddressed or, in ongoing relationships, by signalling that the behaviour is acceptable. Forgiveness performed as an obligation is not the version the benefits attach to.

Treating forgiveness as the same thing as reconciling, excusing, forgetting, or staying in a harmful situation is a category error the research is explicit about avoiding. You can release resentment for your own sake while keeping clear boundaries, ending contact, or fully holding the other person accountable — and in cases of ongoing harm, prioritising safety comes first.

Suppressing or 'just getting over' the hurt without actually acknowledging it tends not to deliver forgiveness's benefits and can resemble avoidance. The work suggests the harm generally needs to be faced honestly first; pretending it did not affect you is different from genuinely releasing resentment about it.
realNumbersInContext: This is an area where the honest move is to hedge: most of the evidence is correlational, effect sizes are generally modest, and forgiveness is hard to measure cleanly, so it would be misleading to attach a precise figure to 'how much forgiveness helps.' What the research supports is a consistent direction — forgiveness is associated with lower anxiety, depression, and stress, and with some better physical-health markers, plausibly by reducing rumination and chronic resentment.

The most important number-free point is the definition. The benefits in this research attach to forgiveness understood as releasing resentment for your own sake — not as excusing, forgetting, reconciling, or staying in an unsafe situation — and forced or premature forgiveness can backfire. Read that way, the finding is less a verdict that you should forgive and more an observation that, when it is genuine and unforced, letting go of resentment tends to be good for the person who does it.

faqs.question: Does forgiving someone actually benefit me?
faqs.answer: The research broadly suggests it tends to, for the forgiver: forgiveness is linked to lower anxiety, depression, and stress, and to some better physical-health markers. A likely reason is that it reduces rumination and chronic resentment. Effects are generally modest and much of the evidence is correlational, but the direction is fairly consistent.

faqs.question: Does forgiving mean excusing what they did or letting them back in?
faqs.answer: No. In this research, forgiveness means releasing resentment for your own sake — not excusing the harm, forgetting it, reconciling, or staying in an unsafe situation. You can let go of resentment while keeping firm boundaries, ending contact, or holding the person fully accountable.

faqs.question: What if I'm not ready to forgive?
faqs.answer: That's worth taking seriously. Some research finds that forced or premature forgiveness can backfire, leaving anger unaddressed or signalling that harmful behaviour is acceptable. Forgiveness in this work is treated as a gradual process, not an obligation, and acknowledging the harm honestly usually comes first.

faqs.question: How does forgiveness actually help, if the other person isn't involved?
faqs.answer: Much of the proposed benefit comes from inside you, not from the other person. Holding an unresolved grievance tends to keep it replaying — sustaining stress over time — and releasing the resentment appears to interrupt that loop. That's why you can get the benefit even with someone you'll never see again.

faqs.question: What is the REACH model of forgiveness?
faqs.answer: It's a structured framework developed by Everett Worthington that treats forgiveness as a gradual process — recalling the hurt honestly, building empathy or understanding where possible, and committing to release resentment over time. The emphasis is on doing it for the forgiver's own benefit, not on absolving the offender.

dataSources: Worthington, E. L. — forgiveness research and the REACH forgiveness model.
Toussaint, L. L., and colleagues — research linking forgiveness to mental and physical health.
